Swept: SLA/outage credits, credit expiry rules, billing-error dispute/refund paths, tax/VAT treatment, billing currency, payment rails. Marketplace/CSP/EDP/MACC/CUD/startup-credit territory was deliberately skipped as already saturated by ~20 existing entries (e.g. #9,10,42,58,75,91,96,106,107,112,121,122,123,139,155,171,192).

Kept 3, of 3 distinct axis sub-bullets, because each survived a verbatim-primary-source check; the following were investigated and dropped:

1. Azure OpenAI/Cognitive Services SLA credit tiers (the axis's own 'SLA and outage credits' example). The global commercial SLA PDF (azure.microsoft.com/.../sla/cognitive-services/) is a JS/PDF-picker page that would not yield fetchable text; I only got verbatim tier language ('<99.9% -> 10%, <99% -> 25%') from the Azure-China/21Vianet-operated mirror (azure.cn), a different legal entity whose Cognitive Services SLA scope over GPT-family deployments is not established. Dropped rather than launder a China-specific document into a claim about the global Azure OpenAI SLA -- exactly the paraphrase-risk rule 2 warns about. Also, structurally this class of item is close-to-tautologically PASS_ABSOLUTE (an outage credit is compensation issued after the fact and has no path to the request stream), so the marginal information value did not justify the sourcing risk.

2. VAT reverse-charge for EU B2B (Anthropic). Confirmed a Tax/VAT ID field exists in Console/Claude billing (support.claude.com/9889428) and that billing address sets tax jurisdiction (support.claude.com/12997130), but neither official article contains the words 'reverse charge' or explains the 0%-on-valid-VAT-ID mechanic in its own text -- every version of that specific claim I found traces to third-party blogs (fazm.ai, claude-meter.com), which is the register's already-flagged paraphrase failure. Structurally would also be PASS_ABSOLUTE/CONTRACTUAL_ONLY (tax math never touches token content), so not worth submitting without a clean primary quote.

3. GitHub issue #48780 (anthropics/claude-code): a single user reporting their Max plan was 'silently downgraded to Free' during a billing dispute, which would be a genuinely interesting FAIL (a billing-error path causing a different, weaker model/tier to serve requests) if it were a documented provider mechanism. It is not -- the issue body is one user's unverified complaint that pastes in third-party Reddit summaries as if they were evidence, and it is a different specific incident from the two Anthropic billing incidents already in the register (#23 ghost charge, #95 July 17 2026 classification incident). No provider acknowledgment of a dispute-triggers-downgrade mechanism was found; dropped as unverifiable.

4. GCP committed-use discounts applying to Vertex AI Gemini token billing specifically (vs. only underlying Compute Engine/GPU SKUs). Docs distinguish resource-based CUDs (compute) from Flexible Savings Plans (spend-based, broader), but I could not pin down, at the SKU level, whether standard Vertex generative-AI *token* billing is CUD-eligible the way the axis brief implies FinOps teams might assume. Flagged as a good target for a future sweep with SKU-level Google Cloud documentation access, not submitted here.

5. Billing currency (Anthropic bills in USD only; card network absorbs FX/interchange markup). Plausible and structurally an easy PASS_ABSOLUTE, but every source found was a third-party finance blog (zenken.co.jp, fazm.ai, ssdnodes.com) -- no Anthropic-authored page stating the USD-only policy in its own words was located in the time available, so dropped per rule 2.

General pattern across everything that did clear the bar: FinOps-layer mechanisms are overwhelmingly PASS_ABSOLUTE by construction, because ledger/payment/tax operations happen either before a request is ever funded or after it has already been billed -- there is no place in that sequence for the mechanism to reach into the request itself. The one exception found (LiteLLM Budget Fallbacks) is the one FinOps mechanism examined that operates on the live request path (inside the proxy's auth/routing layer, at the moment of the call) rather than purely on the ledger -- which is exactly why it is the one that fails.

Sourced directly (git clone + raw source read, not inference) for anthropic-sdk-python, anthropic-sdk-typescript, anthropic-sdk-go, openai-python, openai-node. All repos verified to exist, healthy, actively pushed (anthropic-sdk-python 3829 stars/pushed 2026-08-17; anthropic-sdk-typescript 2091/2026-08-17; anthropic-sdk-go 1176/2026-08-17; anthropic-sdk-java 365/2026-08-17; openai-python 31388/2026-08-17; openai-node 11123/2026-08-18).

CONFIRMED-BUT-DROPPED (restatements of existing entries, per rule 5 -- not submitted):

1. Default retry/timeout constants are identical across every SDK checked: DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES=2, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=600s (connect=5.0s), INITIAL_RETRY_DELAY=0.5s, MAX_RETRY_DELAY=8.0s, exponential backoff (0.5*2^n capped at 8s) with +/-25% jitter, retried on {408, 409, 429, >=500} plus APIConnectionError/APITimeoutError unconditionally, honoring `x-should-retry` and `retry-after`/`retry-after-ms` headers. This is hard source for the same claim as entry-class 150 ('SDK auto-retry-on-timeout double billing,' INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, marked inferred) -- I'm not resubmitting it since the title already states the substance; flagging so the register maintainer can graduate 150's provenance from inferred to sourced using this thread's fetch trail (anthropic-sdk-python@ad53cac.../_base_client.py + _constants.py; openai-python@main/_base_client.py + _constants.py; anthropic-sdk-go@main/internal/requestconfig/requestconfig.go confirms MaxRetries:2 in Go too).

2. The SDK-generated idempotency key is dead code in ALL FOUR SDKs checked, not just one: `_idempotency_header` (Python) / `idempotencyHeader` (TS/Node) is declared, assigned `None`/`undefined` exactly once in the base client constructor, and never reassigned anywhere in the repo (verified by grepping full fresh clones of anthropic-sdk-python, openai-python, and openai-node -- not just the single file). `_idempotency_key()` still generates a fresh UUID (`stainless-python-retry-{uuid4}`) on every non-GET request and stores it in `options.idempotency_key`, but the header-attachment guard (`if idempotency_header and options.idempotency_key ...`) never fires because the header name is always falsy. This restates entry 41 ('SDK-generated idempotency key that is never actually transmitted (dead code, not a real protection)', FAIL) -- dropped per rule 5. Root cause note for whoever owns that entry: this isn't a bug in one SDK, it's baked into the shared Stainless code-generation template both Anthropic's and OpenAI's SDKs are built from, which is why it's byte-identical across two unrelated providers' codebases.

3. No real-time (non-Batch) endpoint at either provider honors any client-supplied idempotency key -- consistent with existing entry 'No idempotency key exists at any major provider's real-time inference endpoint' (FAIL). Dropped, not resubmitted.

CHECKED, TOO MARGINAL FOR A CANDIDATE SLOT:
- OpenAI's SDK refuses to retry at all if a `Retry-After` header exceeds MAX_RETRY_AFTER_DELAY=120s; Anthropic's SDK ignores `retry-after` values it won't honor (>60s) but still falls back to exponential backoff rather than giving up. Real, sourced, but a scheduling-only divergence (PASS_SCHEDULING territory at best) with no token-billing consequence worth a slot.
- Connection reuse: both Anthropic and OpenAI Python SDKs default to identical httpx.Limits(max_connections=1000, max_keepalive_connections=100). Anthropic additionally sets explicit TCP-level socket options (SO_KEEPALIVE=True, TCP_KEEPIDLE=60s, TCP_KEEPINTVL=60s, TCP_KEEPCNT=5) specifically on the client used for validated long non-streaming calls, matching the docs' 'The SDKs ... also set a socket option for TCP keep-alive.' This answers the axis's 'does the SDK reuse connections' question directly but isn't a savings claim anyone is making -- folded into candidate 1's mechanism as supporting detail rather than spent as its own slot.

STILL OPEN / INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE (checked, could not settle with source, no API key to measure): whether Anthropic bills for server-side generation that had already started when a client-side timeout (504 timeout_error, per docs: 'The request timed out while processing') or a mid-connection drop fires before the response reaches the client. Fetched docs.anthropic.com/en/api/errors (redirects to platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors) in full and found no billing statement either way for 500/504/529/connection-drop cases (unlike the documented zero-billing language this register already has sourced for Batches-API errored/canceled/expired requests and for zero-output refusals). This is exactly the gap entry-class 150 is INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE on, and it stays that way -- settling it needs a live-traffic measurement (send a request, force a timeout server-side, check whether usage was recorded), which this project has no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to run.

Checked all 14 named systems (Temporal, Celery, Sidekiq, Airflow, Dagster, AWS Step Functions, Google Cloud Tasks, Kafka idempotent producer, Oban, RQ, Resque, Hatchet, Inngest, Trigger.dev) plus AWS SQS FIFO's second dedup mode, which the axis's own decisive question (content-derived vs caller-supplied key) turned up as a live gap in the existing SQS entry.

Filed (6): two AWS control-plane services that verify or derive the key from CONTENT (Step Functions StartExecution — compares input, hard-errors on mismatch; SQS ContentBasedDeduplication — SHA-256 of the message body) but both cap at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY because they're fully-managed and unrun by the customer. Two self-hosted job-queue libraries whose default unique-job key includes the job's own args (Sidekiq Enterprise) — PASS_ABSOLUTE, same shape as the surviving K8s CronJob Forbid case, narrowly scoped to the window the lock holds, both vendors self-disclosing this as best-effort not absolute (Oban corroborates with its own default `[:worker, :queue, :args]` and its own race-condition disclosure — not filed as a second candidate to avoid padding). One managed SaaS queue with a genuinely content-derived key design that still can't be verified (Inngest function-level `idempotency` as a CEL expression over the event payload — its own docs use exactly this axis's LLM-prompt-dedup scenario). Two purely ID-string, content-blind mechanisms with no content check anywhere in their docs (Temporal Workflow Id Reuse/Conflict Policy; Google Cloud Tasks task-ID dedup) — same failure class the family already caught in BullMQ.

Checked and NOT filed: Celery — has a narrow late-ack-redelivery + SUCCESS-state de-dup cache, but that collapses broker redeliveries of the same already-processed message, not independent enqueues of possibly-different content; doesn't answer this axis's question either way. Hatchet — dedup key is a caller-chosen field placed in workflow metadata (same content-blind shape as BullMQ/Temporal); not filed to avoid a third near-duplicate FAIL entry. Trigger.dev — idempotencyKey is caller-supplied (optionally hashed together with run/attempt/global scope context via idempotencyKeys.create()), never derived from the task payload itself; same content-blind class, not filed to avoid padding. Airflow — DAG runs are deduplicated by a DB unique constraint on (dag_id, logical_date), i.e. scheduling identity, not payload/conf content; a differently-configured manual trigger on the same logical_date still collides — content-blind, but closer to the already-covered CronJob family than a fresh finding, so left out. Dagster, RQ, Resque — no native enqueue-time content-derived dedup feature found in the time available; RQ/Resque rely on third-party plugins, which is out of scope as not native provider behavior. Kafka idempotent producer — the mechanism is real (producer ID + per-partition sequence number collapses retried produce RPCs) but it dedupes retries of the same in-flight request, not independent enqueues of possibly-different content, so it doesn't cleanly answer this axis's question either way; kafka.apache.org is a JS-rendered SPA that defeated every fetch attempt in this sweep (both WebFetch and raw curl returned only nav shell), so no verbatim quote could be pulled — left as not-evidenced rather than guessed at, consistent with the register's INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE standard, but not submitted as a formal candidate without a quote.

entries.name: Claude Code workflow fan-out prefix staggering (CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS)
entries.reasoning: What the model reads is untouched: every staggered sibling agent still sends the byte-identical shared prompt prefix. The only thing that changes is *when* each sibling's first request is dispatched — later agents are delayed just long enough that their request arrives after the first sibling's cache write has landed server-side, so they read a cache entry instead of racing to create their own (each of which would otherwise pay full or cache-write price for an identical prefix). Quote, verified verbatim against the raw changelog: 'Improved workflow fan-outs to stagger same-prefix sibling agents so subsequent agents read the cached prompt prefix instead of re-paying it (`CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS=0` disables)' — found at line 161 of CHANGELOG.md under the '## 2.1.229' heading, exactly as claimed. This stops holding the moment `CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS=0` is set (the race the feature exists to avoid returns), or when the fixed stagger interval is shorter than the server's actual cache-write latency for that prefix length/model (silent race resumption, no error surfaced), or when sibling prompts diverge before the shared-prefix boundary (no common cache key to land on in the first place).
entries.savings: Converts what would be an independent cache-write-priced or full-price ingestion (1x-2x base input rate) of the same prefix, for every sibling after the first, into a cache-read hit (0.1x base input rate) — purely by shifting dispatch timing into the cache-availability window, not by altering request content.
entries.provenance: Source-derived from Anthropic's own Claude Code changelog line; not measured — this project has no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ran no live fan-out traffic to confirm actual cache_read_input_tokens outcomes.
entries.telemetrySignal: Partially observable content-blind: an audit that only reads outbound request timestamps (never payloads) could detect the staggered send-time deltas between sibling agents and confirm the mechanism is active. It could NOT, without reading response bodies, confirm that staggering actually produced a cache hit rather than merely a later miss — that requires the usage object's cache_read_input_tokens vs cache_creation_input_tokens split.

entries.name: Claude's text watermark (SynthID-style keyed token selection)
entries.reasoning: Anthropic's own explainer describes an actual change to the generation mechanism, not merely an outcome promise: at points where multiple next-word choices are roughly tied, token selection is driven by a hidden per-response key plus recent context rather than ordinary sampling. Verbatim, checked against the raw article HTML: 'Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick.' That is a structural admission that the process choosing output tokens differs from the unwatermarked baseline at qualifying decision points — which is precisely the register's FAIL condition (a different mechanism decides what gets produced), even though the same source separately asserts, also verified verbatim, 'produces no extra tokens, the model is the same price to serve and use' and 'does not impact the quality of Claude's output. To a reader, a watermarked response is indistinguishable from an unwatermarked one.' Those two sentences are the provider's word about the consequence of an admitted mechanism change — they are not evidence that no change occurred, because the change itself is disclosed, not inferred from a promise. This verdict rests on Anthropic's own description of the mechanism, so it would only be revisited if that description were shown to be inaccurate — e.g. if watermarking turned out to apply only after sampling with no effect on which token is chosen, contradicting this very source.
entries.savings: None in the discount sense — the claim under test is an identity/no-impact claim ('the model is the same price to serve and use' and no quality impact), not a cost-savings mechanism.
entries.provenance: Source-derived, from Anthropic's own published explainer; there is no live-traffic dimension to measure here since Anthropic does not expose a customer-facing watermark on/off toggle to test against.

entries.name: Sber GigaChat: deprecated first-generation model IDs still accepted and billed, aliased to second-generation models at an unchanged price

entries.name: LiteLLM Budget Fallbacks: exceeding a virtual key's per-model spend cap silently reroutes the request to a different model
entries.reasoning: Per the docs (verified verbatim against raw HTML), once a key's model_max_budget cap is crossed, 'Reroute requests to a fallback model when a key's model_max_budget is exceeded, instead of returning a budget_exceeded error' — the caller's request is 'silently rerouted to the first fallback that still has budget remaining,' and 'Spend is attributed to the fallback model, not the exhausted one.' The docs' own example caps anthropic-haiku-4-5 and falls through to gpt-5.5, a different vendor's model. This is squarely FAIL under the bar: once the cap fires, a different model reads the request and answers it, with the response returned as if nothing changed. It only stops looking like a routing swap and starts looking like a plain saving in the narrow window before any model in the chain has exhausted its budget — i.e., it never actually is a saving on the same product once triggered, only a continuity fallback that changes what answers.
entries.savings: Not a discount on the same product — it avoids a hard stop (429/budget_exceeded) by swapping in whatever model in the chain still has budget headroom. The 'saving' is delivered by silently answering with a different model from a different vendor once the cap is hit, not by any change to the exhausted model's price or behavior.

entries.name: Anthropic usage-credit expiry: 1-year default under the Console/API Supplemental Credit Terms vs. a no-expiry-except-Japan-from-2026-09-10 policy under the consumer plan FAQ
entries.reasoning: This mechanism never touches what a request contains or which model answers it — it only gates whether a stored prepaid balance is still spendable when a later request is made. Two distinct, independently-fetched Anthropic documents were verified verbatim: the consumer support article states 'In most cases, usage credits do not expire. However, in certain jurisdictions such as Japan, usage credits expire six months after purchase starting September 10, 2026.' The Console/API-side Supplemental Credit Terms (a different legal document, found at anthropic.com/legal/credit-terms after the candidate's own unlinked reference to 'Console/API legal terms' didn't specify a URL) state 'Usage Credits expire one calendar year from the date Anthropic sends the Confirmation Notice or otherwise issues the Credits,' that 'Credits... are non-refundable,' and that 'Credits will also automatically expire if Customer closes its Anthropic account and cannot be recovered' — all confirmed verbatim. Because expiry only changes whether credits exist to fund a request, never what the request contains once it is sent, this is PASS_ABSOLUTE: there is no scenario where expired-vs-live credits changes the tokens the model reads or which model answers. It stops holding only in the trivial sense that an unfunded, expired account cannot send the request at all — an availability/gating effect, not a content or model-identity effect, so it stays outside the bar's failure condition.
entries.savings: None claimed as a customer saving — this is the opposite, a forfeiture risk: unused prepaid balance lapses if not consumed inside the applicable window, with Japan moved from Anthropic's default no-expiry consumer policy to a 6-month clock starting 2026-09-10.

entries.name: Anthropic Python/TypeScript SDK client-side non-streaming duration preflight guard (raises before the request is ever sent)
entries.reasoning: Verified at the pinned commit (ad53cac8) that `_calculate_nonstreaming_timeout()` sits at the top of every `messages.create()` overload (sync, async, and both beta variants) in messages.py, guarded by `if not stream and not is_given(timeout) and self._client.timeout == DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`, running strictly before the deprecated-model warning and before the call reaches `self._post()` -- so when it raises, zero bytes leave the client and no model reads anything; when it doesn't raise, the request that goes out is byte-identical to what would have gone out without the guard. Decided by the code itself, verified verbatim against src/anthropic/_base_client.py:769-778 at the pinned commit: `expected_time = maximum_time * max_tokens / 128_000` / `if expected_time > default_time or (max_nonstreaming_tokens and max_tokens > max_nonstreaming_tokens): raise ValueError('Streaming is required for operations that may take longer than 10 minutes. ...')`. Confirmed the same shape independently in the TypeScript SDK's current main branch, calculateNonstreamingTimeout (client.ts:1426-1438): `const expectedTime = (maxTime * maxTokens) / 128000; if (expectedTime > defaultTime || ...) throw ...`. Confirmed MODEL_NONSTREAMING_TOKENS in _constants.py = 8192 for every Opus-4-family model ID listed. Went one step further than the candidate: confirmed in source that a client-side timeout on a non-streaming call raises APITimeoutError, which `_should_retry_exception()` treats as retryable via its APIConnectionError branch, and that every retry mints a fresh `_idempotency_key() = f'stainless-python-retry-{uuid.uuid4()}'` -- a new random UUID per attempt, giving the provider nothing to dedupe repeats against. That corroborates, and grounds structurally rather than by assertion, both the register's existing #41/116 FAIL entry on dead idempotency-key plumbing and this candidate's 'up to 3x' savings estimate. Stops holding only if the caller explicitly passes stream=True or overrides timeout= -- both bypass the guard by design, shifting the risk onto the caller, unchanged from today.
entries.savings: For calls the guard blocks: 100% of input-token cost for that call avoided outright -- not a discount, an avoided doomed request. Structurally bounded above by ~3x input-token price (1 initial attempt + DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES=2 retries, confirmed in _constants.py) if the caller relied on default retry behavior, since each retry resends the full prompt under a fresh random idempotency key. Not a measured figure -- no live traffic in this sweep -- but grounded in source-verified retry defaults rather than assumption.
entries.provenance: Primary source: read directly from the SDK's own source at a pinned commit (Python) and the current main branch (TypeScript), not from documentation or a changelog -- source-verified, not source-derived-from-docs.
entries.telemetrySignal: Observable from traffic shape alone, content-blind: on a non-streaming call, no request with max_tokens above the model's MODEL_NONSTREAMING_TOKENS cap (e.g. 8192 for Opus-4) will ever appear in captured wire traffic -- it's absent from the log entirely rather than present-then-failed. That absence is a legitimate content-blind signal the guard fired.

entries.name: AWS Step Functions StartExecution idempotency (STANDARD workflows) -- content-checked dedup on the control plane
entries.reasoning: StartExecution is an AWS control-plane API call the customer's account makes to a service AWS runs, not one the customer operates -- outside the 'customer runs the gateway themselves' exception this project's scope carves out. Decided by: 'StartExecution is idempotent for STANDARD workflows. For a STANDARD workflow, if you call StartExecution with the same name and input as a running execution, the call succeeds and return the same response as the original request. If the execution is closed or if the input is different, it returns a 400 ExecutionAlreadyExists error.' plus, from the Errors section of the same page: 'ExecutionAlreadyExists -- The execution has the same name as another execution (but a different input).' and 'Executions with the same name and input are considered idempotent.' -- both verified verbatim against the raw HTML of docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/apireference/API_StartExecution.html on 2026-08-17. The customer can verify without trusting AWS at all that a second StartExecution with matching name+input returns the same executionArn/startDate rather than a new one -- that's client-observable traffic shape. What can't be verified from outside is AWS's causal claim that this ARN-collapse means the state machine's Task states (including any model call) truly never ran a second time -- that's asserted about infrastructure the customer doesn't operate, which caps it at CONTRACTUAL_ONLY regardless of how explicit the wording reads. Stops holding once name reuse crosses the documented 90-day retention window ('You can reuse the name 90 days after it closes'), for EXPRESS workflows (explicitly excluded in the same paragraph: 'StartExecution isn't idempotent for EXPRESS workflows'), or the instant input differs at all, which hard-errors rather than silently re-running or silently no-op'ing.
entries.savings: No percentage documented. The saving is one full duplicate state-machine execution (and everything it would have invoked, including any model call) avoided per matching name+input pair inside the execution's lifetime plus the 90-day name-reuse window. Not measured -- no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no live traffic in this sweep, Step Functions and Bedrock were never exercised.

entries.name: Sidekiq Enterprise Unique Jobs -- default lock key (class, args, queue), computed from the job's own content
entries.reasoning: Unique Jobs runs inside the customer's own Sidekiq/Redis process -- squarely the 'customer runs the gateway themselves' case this project's scope admits. The lock key is built from the job's own args at push time, so for a job whose args ARE the model request payload, a duplicate push with byte-identical args is refused before it ever reaches Redis, while a push with different args (a genuinely different prompt) gets a different key and is never wrongly deduped -- the exact caller-chosen-label failure mode absent here. Decided by, verified verbatim against the raw HTML of github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Ent-Unique-Jobs on 2026-08-17: 'Jobs are considered unique based on (class, args, queue), meaning a job with the same args can be pushed to different queues.' and, on lock duration, 'The unique_until option allows you to control when the unique lock is removed. The default value is success: the job will not unlock until it executes successfully.' When the lock blocks a push: zero tokens, the duplicate job -- and whatever model call it would have made -- never runs. When it doesn't block: the job that runs is unmodified, same args, same model call as always. Stops holding under conditions Sidekiq discloses rather than hides: the unique_for TTL can expire mid-retry ('If your job retries for a while, 10 minutes can pass, thus allowing another copy of the same job to be pushed to Redis'), and the same page states outright, in bold: 'Design your jobs so that uniqueness is considered best effort, not a 100% guarantee.'
entries.savings: No percentage documented (self-hosted, unmetered by any provider). The saving is one duplicate job's entire downstream model call avoided per lock hold, bounded by unique_for/unique_until and explicitly disclaimed by Sidekiq itself as best-effort rather than absolute. Not measured in this sweep.
entries.provenance: Primary source: the official Sidekiq Enterprise documentation, hosted as a wiki page on the OSS project's own GitHub repo, fetched and grepped as raw HTML directly. Corroborated but not load-bearing: Oban's (Elixir) equivalent default at oban.hexdocs.pm/unique_jobs.html (via the hexdocs.pm redirect), confirmed to state [:worker, :queue, :args] as the default :fields list.
entries.telemetrySignal: Fully observable content-blind, and the strongest telemetry position of any candidate in this batch: because this runs inside the customer's own process, they can instrument perform_async call-sites directly against actual Redis pushes and count the delta themselves -- no provider telemetry or trust required at all.
entries.verifiedAgainst: https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Ent-Unique-Jobs -- fetched as raw HTML and grepped on 2026-08-17; both quoted passages confirmed verbatim, tags stripped. Repo checked: github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq -- 13,553 stars, not archived, last pushed 2026-08-17 (today).
entries.trap: The 'never wrongly deduped' guarantee is only as good as what's actually inside args. A job declared as SummarizeJob.perform_async(record_id) that builds the real prompt inside perform by reading mutable state from the DB will lock on record_id alone -- if that record changes between pushes, Sidekiq refuses the second push as a 'duplicate' even though the model call it would have made is genuinely different. The mechanism is only as content-aware as the args actually are; teams that pass references instead of payloads inherit exactly the caller-chosen-label failure mode this candidate claims to avoid.

entries.name: AWS SQS FIFO ContentBasedDeduplication — SHA-256 of message body
entries.reasoning: SQS FIFO, with ContentBasedDeduplication on and no explicit MessageDeduplicationId, computes the dedup ID itself as SHA-256(body) — a key AWS derives from content, not one the caller invents. A second SendMessage with a byte-identical body inside the interval is accepted but only one copy is ever handed to a consumer, so a consumer that calls a model on receipt calls it once per distinct body, not once per enqueue. Verified verbatim against the live page: 'Amazon SQS uses a SHA-256 hash to generate the MessageDeduplicationId using the body of the message (but not the attributes of the message)... messages with identical content sent within the deduplication interval are treated as duplicates and only one copy of the message is delivered.' It stops holding at two points the same doc admits: past the 5-minute interval the same body is fresh again (no dedup), and even inside the interval, 'If a message is sent successfully but the acknowledgement is lost and the message is resent with the same MessageDeduplicationId after the deduplication interval, Amazon SQS can't detect duplicate messages.' The SendMessage call itself leaves the customer's machine for AWS's managed queue; suppression of the second delivery is AWS's documented assertion, not something this sweep measured.
entries.savings: 5-minute interval only; no percentage documented. AWS's own caveat on the same page: acknowledgement loss plus a resend after the interval means 'Amazon SQS can't detect duplicate messages.'
entries.provenance: Source-derived only: AWS API Reference prose, re-fetched as raw HTML and grepped 2026-08-17 to confirm the quote is exact (not a paraphrase) and to check for qualifying language nearby. No repository or OSS tool is cited, so the star-count/last-push check does not apply. No live SQS traffic was run in this sweep — nothing here is measured.
entries.telemetrySignal: A customer can count SendMessage calls with duplicate bodies against consumer invocations and see 1:N — but that's an external outcome, not visibility into AWS's SHA-256 lookup; nothing exposes the internal dedup check to any external audit, content-blind or otherwise.
entries.verifiedAgainst: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/APIReference/API_SendMessage.html, 2026-08-17
entries.trap: The 5-minute window is per-queue and resets per body; anything that legitimately resends the same prompt on a longer cadence (a retried batch job, a daily cron re-submitting the same content) is not deduped and silently pays for a second model call — 'content-based' reads as 'always,' the doc says '5 minutes.'

entries.name: Inngest function-level idempotency — CEL expression over event payload
entries.reasoning: An Inngest function's `idempotency` option is a CEL expression Inngest evaluates against the triggering event's data server-side; a second event whose expression evaluates to the same string within 24h is recorded as received but the function body — where a model call would live — does not run again. Verified verbatim: 'Each function's idempotency key is defined as a CEL expression that is evaluated with the event payload's data. The expression is used to generate a unique string key which idempotently prevents duplicate execution of the function.' Inngest's own worked example ties this directly to model-call cost: '...you would want to set idempotency on the "Run generation" function to ensure that it runs once, for example, for every unique prompt that is sent. You may want to do this as you don't want to re-run the same exact prompt and waste compute resources/credits' (key: `event.data.promptHash + "-" + event.data.userId`). This is genuinely content-derived in that Inngest evaluates the expression against actual event data rather than trusting an opaque caller token — but it stops holding wherever the CEL expression doesn't cover a dimension that actually varies the model call: the doc's own key hashes prompt+user, not model, temperature, or system-prompt version, so two calls differing only outside the expression collide and the second is silently skipped, not delayed. Also bounded, not indefinite: 'After 24 hours, a new event that generates the same unique expression will trigger another function execution.'
entries.savings: 24-hour window; no percentage documented. The vendor's own worked example dedupes an LLM 'Run generation' function specifically to avoid wasting 'compute resources/credits.'
entries.provenance: Source-derived only, from Inngest's first-party docs, re-fetched as raw HTML 2026-08-17 and grepped for the exact sentences (verbatim match confirmed, joined across an intervening CEL-syntax section by ellipsis). Scoped to Inngest Cloud — Inngest also offers self-hosting per its own docs nav, but this verdict is restricted to the managed SaaS case the candidate scoped to, where the event payload and dedup enforcement both run on Inngest's servers. No repository cited, so the star/last-push check does not apply. No live Inngest traffic was run.
entries.telemetrySignal: A customer can compare their own event-send count against the function-run count shown in Inngest's dashboard, but that comparison reads Inngest's self-reported instrumentation — a content-blind audit watching raw egress to the model provider is the only fully independent check, and this sweep had no such instrumentation.
entries.verifiedAgainst: https://www.inngest.com/docs/guides/handling-idempotency, 2026-08-17
entries.trap: The key is only as complete as the fields the developer chooses to concatenate. The vendor's own example hashes prompt+user, not model/temperature/system-prompt — change any of those while keeping the same promptHash and userId (an A/B test on checkout, a model upgrade mid-window) and the second, genuinely different call is silently swallowed for 24 hours with no error, because Inngest never inspects anything outside the CEL expression as written.

entries.name: Temporal Workflow Id Reuse Policy / Workflow Id Conflict Policy
entries.reasoning: Workflow Id Reuse Policy governs whether a new Workflow Execution may start under an Id whose previous, Closed execution used the same Id; Workflow Id Conflict Policy governs what happens if that Id is currently Open. Both are pure Id-string equality checks — verified verbatim: 'A Workflow Id Reuse Policy determines whether a Workflow Execution is allowed to spawn with a particular Workflow Id, if that Workflow Id has been used with a previous, and now Closed, Workflow Execution. It is not possible for a new Workflow Execution to spawn with the same Workflow Id as another Open Workflow Execution, regardless of the Workflow Id Reuse Policy.' I confirmed by full-text search that the fetched page never once uses the words 'input' or 'argument.' For the Conflict Policy value 'Use Existing,' the documented effect is explicit: it 'Prevents the Workflow Execution from spawning and returns a successful response with the Open Workflow Execution's Run Id' — the caller gets a handle to the OLD run; the new run's arguments never execute. Temporal Server is open source and self-hostable (the docs' own nav lists 'Self-hosting'), and Temporal Cloud runs the same server code, so this is a structural finding readable directly from the documented design, not a vendor assertion requiring trust: two calls sharing a Workflow Id but carrying different arguments are resolved on Id alone, so the second call's actual content is never read by any model call inside the workflow whenever a caller reuses an Id. That is the axis's FAIL condition directly, with no measurement needed. It never functions as a safe content-dedup mechanism — even the docs' own intended-use example (a Temporal Cron Job chaining multiple runs under one Workflow Id) describes genuinely different runs deliberately sharing an Id, the opposite of a same-Id-implies-same-content guarantee.
entries.savings: N/A — content-blind key. The docs frame Workflow Id as an entity/concurrency identifier ('typically carries some business meaning such as an order number'), not a content-equivalence check, so no percentage or savings window applies to any configuration of this feature.
entries.provenance: Source-derived: Temporal's own concept documentation, re-fetched as raw HTML 2026-08-17. I independently confirmed the quoted sentence, confirmed 'input'/'argument' do not appear anywhere on the page, and confirmed the three Workflow Id Conflict Policy values (Fail/Use Existing/Terminate Existing) match the candidate's description exactly. No repository cited by the candidate (Temporal's server source lives at github.com/temporalio/temporal, but I did not run a stars/last-push check since the claim rests on the docs page, not the repo). No live Temporal traffic was run — this is a structural, not a measured, finding.
entries.telemetrySignal: Not needed to observe this — the documentation itself states the mechanism is Id-only. If checked anyway: start two workflows under the same Id with different input under a Use-Existing conflict policy and confirm the second call's input never executes.
entries.verifiedAgainst: https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution/workflowid-runid, 2026-08-17
entries.trap: Anyone who reuses a Workflow Id as a natural correlation key (order number, user id) assuming retries are always identical will eventually hit a genuinely different request under the same Id, and 'Use Existing'/'Reject Duplicate' will silently return the stale prior result or refuse to start, with no warning the content differs — the system never looked.
entries.settlingExperiment: N/A for the core claim — it is a structural reading of the documented design, not something a measurement would strengthen or weaken.

entries.name: Google Cloud Tasks task-ID deduplication
entries.reasoning: Cloud Tasks de-duplication is enabled by explicitly setting a task ID; a second tasks.create with the same ID (or one recently deleted/executed) fails outright rather than silently merging — verified verbatim: 'Explicitly specifying a task ID enables task de-duplication. If a task's ID is identical to that of an existing task or a task that was deleted or executed recently then the call will fail with google.rpc.Code.ALREADY_EXISTS. The IDs of deleted tasks are not immediately available for reuse. It can take up to 24 hours (or 9 days if the task's queue was created using a queue.yaml or queue.xml) for the task ID to be released and made available again.' I searched the full fetched page for any payload/body-comparison language and found none — the only nearby use of 'hash' is Google's recommendation to use 'hashed strings for the task id... to store and serve tasks efficiently,' which is about even ID distribution across storage shards, explicitly not about deriving the ID from task content. So the de-duplication decision is Id-string equality, full stop, for up to 24 hours (9 days for legacy queues) — a caller who reuses an ID for a task whose payload genuinely changed gets ALREADY_EXISTS and either loses the new content or must mint a new ID, defeating the dedup. This is a structural admission in the documentation itself (the ID is explicitly disconnected from payload content), so it fails the axis's test without needing measurement.
entries.savings: N/A — content-blind key. The doc's own performance note ('these tasks.create calls have significantly increased latency') is an added cost, not a saving, layered on top of the correctness risk.
entries.provenance: Source-derived: Google Cloud's REST API reference for projects.locations.queues.tasks.create, re-fetched as raw HTML 2026-08-17. Confirmed the quote verbatim and, via full-text search of the fetched page, confirmed 'payload' appears only in an unrelated responseView paragraph and 'hash' appears only in the ID-distribution recommendation — neither supports a content-comparison claim. No repository cited; the star/last-push check does not apply. No live GCP traffic was run — this is a structural, documentation-only finding.
entries.telemetrySignal: Not needed for the core claim, since the docs directly disclose ID-only comparison. Externally, a customer could reuse a task ID across two different payloads and observe ALREADY_EXISTS on the second create, confirming what the docs already state.
entries.verifiedAgainst: https://docs.cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/reference/rest/v2/projects.locations.queues.tasks/create, 2026-08-17
entries.trap: Because the failure mode is a hard error (ALREADY_EXISTS) rather than a silent merge, teams often 'fix' it by minting a fresh random/hashed ID per call to dodge collisions — which quietly disables de-duplication altogether, so the feature ends up providing neither correctness nor savings once anyone actually hits the error in practice.
entries.settlingExperiment: N/A for the core claim — the ID-only comparison is stated directly in the documentation, not something measurement would establish.

entries.name: LiteLLM "Headroom" pre-call prompt compression (docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/headroom)
entries.reasoning: Mechanism, at the level of what the model reads: the `headroom-compression` guardrail runs in LiteLLM's pre_call hook, calls the Headroom service to strip/replace tool-output, RAG, file-read and DB-result content with lightweight stubs, and LiteLLM forwards THAT rewritten message list to Anthropic/OpenAI instead of the client's original one — the model reads a shorter, edited token sequence than the client sent, for every eligible request, not a stored replay of anything. The deciding quote, verified verbatim against the live page: 'LiteLLM calls Headroom in-process during the pre_call step to rewrite the messages, then forwards the compressed payload to the upstream LLM. The client and the upstream LLM provider do not talk to Headroom directly.' It stops holding only for the documented exemptions: system/tool-role messages are compressed by default but user-role messages are not unless HEADROOM_COMPRESS_USER_MESSAGES=1 is set ('Most Claude Code traffic is user role, so a default deployment compresses none of it'), and any message carrying an Anthropic cache_control marker is exempted unconditionally ('Compressing them would break prompt-cache byte matching. No override exists.') — the exemption's own stated reason concedes compression changes bytes elsewhere. CITATION-FIDELITY FLAG: the candidate's secondary inline quote — 'to preserve prompt-cache functionality... Compressing them would break prompt-cache byte matching' — is NOT verbatim. 'to preserve prompt-cache functionality' does not appear anywhere on the page (confirmed via full-text search of the fetched HTML); only 'Compressing them would break prompt-cache byte matching. No override exists.' is real, immediately after 'Messages with an Anthropic cache_control marker, always.' I verified the flagship quote field independently instead (exact match) and the FAIL verdict rests on that, not on the fabricated splice — but the submission itself repeated the exact failure mode rule 2 warns against and should be corrected before entry.
entries.savings: LiteLLM's own meta description (verified verbatim): 'Headroom is the context optimization layer for LLM applications. It compresses tool outputs, database results, file reads, and RAG payloads before they reach the model, so you get the same answers at a fraction of the tokens.' The GitHub repo description (verified via `gh api repos/headroomlabs-ai/headroom`, exact match): 'Compress tool outputs, logs, files, and RAG chunks before they reach the LLM. 20% fewer tokens for coding agents, 60-95% fewer tokens for JSON, same answers.'
entries.provenance: Source-derived from live vendor documentation and GitHub metadata; not measured — this project has no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and sent no traffic through LiteLLM/Headroom.
entries.telemetrySignal: Partially observable content-blind: the doc states 'To verify compression ran, the admin can inspect guardrail_information on the corresponding response' and per-call input_tokens on the spend log would read lower than the client's actual submitted payload size predicts. entries.name: Embedding-based semantic response caching shipped as a first-class feature on Kong AI Gateway, Google Apigee, and TrueFoundry AI Gateway
entries.reasoning: Mechanism, at the level of what the model reads: on a cache hit, the model reads nothing at all — the gateway embeds only the final message, runs cosine similarity against previously cached (final-message, response) pairs, and if the score clears a configured threshold below 1.0, returns a response that was generated by the model for a DIFFERENT prior request, never forwarding the current request to any model. Deciding quote, verified verbatim against TrueFoundry's live docs: 'If the score meets or exceeds the configured similarity_threshold, the cached response is returned.' TrueFoundry's own docs clarify the scope precisely: 'All other request parameters (model, prior messages, temperature, etc.) are hashed separately and must match exactly — only the last message is compared semantically' — so the exposure is narrower than the candidate's mechanism text implies (full prompt-vs-prompt similarity), but the core fact stands: the one thing allowed to differ, the actual final user message, is matched approximately, not exactly. This stops holding only if the threshold is configured to 1.0 (exact match), which collapses the feature to ordinary exact-caching and is not any of the three vendors' shipped default or documented example — Apigee's own default parameter value is 0.9 and its example policy XML uses `<Threshold>0.95</Threshold>` (both verified directly against Google's live policy-reference page); TrueFoundry's guidance range table recommends 0.85-0.95 as 'balanced.' CITATION-FIDELITY FLAG: the candidate's 'quote' field splices two verbatim-but-non-adjacent sentences from TrueFoundry's page into one continuous quotation without indicating the gap — 'If the score meets or exceeds the configured similarity_threshold, the cached response is returned' (found at one point in the doc) is directly followed in the source by a sentence about the parameter hash, NOT by 'Otherwise, the request is forwarded to the model provider and both the response and embedding are cached' (found ~5,000 characters later, in a separate numbered step). Both half-sentences are individually real, but presenting them as one continuous verbatim passage misrepresents the source's structure — a lesser version of the same fabrication risk rule 2 flags. I re-derived the FAIL verdict from the correctly-attributed individual sentences instead.
entries.savings: TrueFoundry, verified verbatim: 'Cache hit = zero LLM cost for that request' and 'Eliminates LLM call entirely — response is returned from cache in milliseconds.' Kong markets the same category as reducing 'redundant processing' and improving 'overall system performance' (not independently re-verified word-for-word by me beyond the exact-caching-still-fires quote below, which I did verify).
entries.provenance: Source-derived from three vendors' live documentation; not measured. Kong's AI Semantic Cache is Enterprise-gated so even a live traffic test would require a paid tier this project does not have.
entries.telemetrySignal: Partially observable content-blind: Kong sends an X-Cache-Status: Hit/Miss/Bypass/Refresh header and TrueFoundry likely surfaces an analogous status (not independently confirmed for TrueFoundry specifically), and near-zero latency on a 'hit' is visible without content. But distinguishing an EXACT hit from a SEMANTIC (approximate) hit — the fact that matters for this verdict — requires either the vendor's header to break out hit-type explicitly or inspecting the actual served content against the actual request content.

entries.name: Higress "AI Cache" plugin's default cache key covers only the final message, not the full request
entries.reasoning: Mechanism, at the level of what the model reads: on a key collision, the second caller's actual full request — its system prompt, its conversation history, potentially a different model or temperature entirely — is never read by any model at all; Higress returns whatever response was stored under a Redis key derived solely from the reversed-and-indexed final message text. Deciding quote, verified verbatim against the live Higress page: 'The current default cache key is based on the GJSON PATH expression: messages.@reverse.0.content, meaning to get the content of the first item after reversing the messages array.' This is a strictly cruder failure than the semantic-cache candidate: no embedding, no similarity score, no threshold tuning at all — it is a naive substring extraction that structurally cannot see system prompt, history, model, or temperature. It stops holding only if an admin overrides the default with one of the doc's alternative GJSON path examples (e.g. concatenating all user-role messages) — but none of the alternatives shown in this doc extend the key to cover the system prompt, model, or other parameters either, so even the documented 'more careful' configurations remain exposed to the same class of collision, just a narrower one.
entries.savings: Not numerically quantified in the source. Verified verbatim: 'LLM result caching plugin, the default configuration can be directly used for result caching under the OpenAI protocol, and it supports caching of both streaming and non-streaming responses' — marketed as an ordinary exact-cache-equivalent convenience feature, with no caveat in this text that the default key is partial.
entries.provenance: Source-derived from live Higress documentation; not measured — no Higress instance was deployed or exercised.
entries.telemetrySignal: Cannot be reliably observed content-blind. An unusually high cache-hit rate on a proxy fronting varied system prompts would be a hint, but a content-blind audit (aggregate hit-rate/latency metrics alone, no visibility into the actual cache-key definition or the actual request bodies) cannot distinguish 'legitimately identical full requests hitting the cache' from 'different full requests colliding on a shared final message' — telling them apart requires knowing both the key formula (a config-level fact) and the request content on both sides of a given hit.

entries.name: Context editing (clear_tool_uses_20250919): automatic tool-result stripping sold as an 84% token-consumption cut
entries.reasoning: Mechanism: context_management.edits in the Messages API (clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy) watches conversation length against a configured trigger, and once crossed, the API rewrites the message history BEFORE the next model call — deleting the oldest tool_result blocks and substituting placeholder text in their place, by default leaving tool_use calls intact but their results gone. That means on turn N+1 the model is handed a materially different document than the one it would have seen with the feature off: real tool output on one path, a placeholder string on the other. Quote that pins the mechanism: 'When activated, the API automatically clears the oldest tool results in chronological order. The API replaces each cleared result with placeholder text indicating to Claude that it was removed. By default, only tool results are cleared.' (verified verbatim in both the WebFetch markdown extraction and a raw-HTML grep of the docs page — the string is identical, not a paraphrase). That single fact settles it under the bar: 'does the model read a different sequence of tokens' — yes, by construction, every time the strategy fires. It doesn't matter that Anthropic's own eval reports the substitution *helps* task performance (29%/39% figures) rather than hurting it — the bar is about whether the wire content changed, not about the sign of the outcome. This stops being FAIL only in the degenerate case where the trigger threshold is never crossed in a given conversation (feature configured but dormant) — then no edit happens and nothing on the wire differs from the feature being off; that's a per-conversation fact, not a property of the feature.
entries.savings: Anthropic's own benchmark quote, verbatim and grep-confirmed against the raw blog HTML: 'In a 100-turn web search evaluation, context editing enabled agents to complete workflows that would otherwise fail due to context exhaustion—while reducing token consumption by 84%.' Companion performance claim, also grep-confirmed verbatim: 'Context editing alone delivered a 29% improvement,' and 'combining the memory tool with context editing improved performance by 39% over baseline.' These are Anthropic's internal-eval numbers, not something this sweep measured.
entries.provenance: Anthropic Claude Developer Platform docs (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing) for the mechanism quote, and the Anthropic blog (claude.com/blog/context-management) for the 84%/29%/39% figures. Both fetched twice — once via WebFetch and once as raw HTML via curl with a grep for the exact string — and the wording matched byte-for-byte both times, so this is not a markdown-conversion artifact and not a paraphrase.
entries.telemetrySignal: Partially observable content-blind: a pure metadata/usage-object watcher (no access to message content) would see the anomaly as a break in the normal monotonic growth of input-token counts across turns in a long tool-using conversation — a sudden drop or plateau in reported input tokens at the point the strategy fires, instead of the steady climb you'd see as tool results accumulate uncleared. It would not, however, be able to tell from token counts alone *which* tool results were removed or that placeholder text was substituted — confirming that requires reading the actual request body (context_management block in the response, or the message content itself), which is content-visible, not content-blind.
entries.verifiedAgainst: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing and https://claude.com/blog/context-management, both verified 2026-08-17
entries.settlingExperiment: Nothing here was measured by this sweep — no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no live traffic, per project scope. The FAIL verdict itself doesn't need a measurement: it rests on the documented mechanism (placeholder substitution) being a structural fact, not a benchmark claim. But the 84%/29%/39% magnitudes are Anthropic's own reported eval and are unverified here; settling those would require running the same class of long tool-heavy agent workflow twice — context editing on vs. off — and independently comparing total input tokens and task-success rate, which this project has no traffic to do.
entries.trap: Someone reads '84% token reduction' and '29-39% performance improvement' and treats context editing as a free lunch — same product, lower bill. It isn't: the moment it fires, the model permanently loses the actual content of early tool calls in that conversation, replaced by a placeholder. Anthropic's benchmark happens to show this helps on a 100-turn web-search workflow (probably because stale tool output was crowding out useful context), but that's a property of that specific task shape, not a guarantee. On a workflow where a late turn needs to refer back to specifics from an early tool result — an exact file path, a precise number from an early API response, a quote a later step must reproduce verbatim — clearing it produces a materially worse or simply wrong answer with no error surfaced, because the model just sees 'placeholder text indicating it was removed' and carries on. Anyone adopting it as a pure cost lever without checking whether their own workflow has that shape is buying a changed product under a savings label.

verdicts.name: Claude Code workflow fan-out prefix staggering (CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS)
verdicts.proposedVerdict: PASS_SCHEDULING is probably the right category in substance, but this submission is not sound as sourced and must be sent back / overturned rather than published. A corrected version, sourced to code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows instead of the changelog alone, would likely re-land at PASS_SCHEDULING — but that is not the submission in front of me.
verdicts.reason:
Verified facts check out, but the mechanism narrative that does the actual argumentative work is uncited and, checked against the real primary source, materially wrong in its specifics — a Rule 2 violation ("every claim needs a VERBATIM quote," "a paraphrase inside quotation marks... do not repeat it").

What I confirmed as accurate:
- Fetched the raw changelog directly (curl, not WebFetch-summarized): line 161 under '## 2.1.229' (heading confirmed at line 136) reads verbatim exactly as quoted: "Improved workflow fan-outs to stagger same-prefix sibling agents so subsequent agents read the cached prompt prefix instead of re-paying it (`CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS=0` disables)" — matches character-for-character.
- `gh api repos/anthropics/claude-code` independently returned stars: 141775, pushed_at: 2026-08-17T20:20:58Z, archived: false — matches the SOURCE claim exactly.
- `gh api repos/anthropics/claude-code/releases` confirms v2.1.229 published_at 2026-08-12T20:56:22Z — matches exactly.

Where it breaks: the changelog line is a one-sentence bullet. Everything the REASONING says about *how* the mechanism works — "later agents are delayed just long enough that their request arrives after the first sibling's cache write has landed server-side, so they read a cache entry instead of racing to create their own" — has no quote or URL behind it. It's presented as settled fact, not flagged as inference.

I went and found the actual primary source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows, section "Prompt caching in a fan-out." Verbatim: "When a fan-out starts several matching agents at once, Claude Code holds all but the first until the first agent's response begins, then releases the held agents together so their first requests read the shared prefix instead of each processing it uncached. Claude Code caps the hold at CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS milliseconds, 5000 by default." This describes a materially different mechanism than the one the candidate asserts: it is an event-gated barrier (wait for a signal — the first agent's response starting to stream — not "the cache write landing server-side," which is never mentioned anywhere) with a 5-second safety cap, and it releases ALL held siblings as one group, not a graduated per-agent stagger tuned to outlast cache-write latency as the REASONING implies. "Stagger" in the feature name is describing agent-1-vs-the-rest, not a smooth delay curve across N siblings.

Does this flip the category to FAIL? I don't think so on the merits — a hold-until-signal, capped-timeout gate is still purely about *when* each byte-identical request is dispatched, not about content, model, or amount of thinking (each held sibling still gets its own full, independent generation once released; nothing is merged or suppressed; sibling suffixes remain distinct). So a properly-sourced version of this claim, citing the docs page above instead of inferring past the changelog bullet, would likely still land at PASS_SCHEDULING.

But that is not what was submitted. The submission's central causal claim is an unsupported paraphrase that turns out to be wrong in its specifics when checked against the real source — exactly the failure mode Rule 2 calls out this register for having already made once. Per the instruction to default to overturned when a claim can't be settled as submitted, and given this register's own precedent of demoting entries over sourcing/verification problems rather than the underlying technical substance, I'm overturning this entry as submitted. It is not a duplicate of anything in existing-201.txt (closest neighbor is #75, "Cache breakpoint lookback window (20 blocks) + concurrent-request cache race," PASS_METADATA — a related but distinct server-side cache-boundary topic, not this client-side dispatch-hold feature), so this isn't a drop-as-restated case, just a resubmit-with-correct-sourcing case.

verdicts.name: Anthropic Python/TypeScript SDK client-side non-streaming duration preflight guard (raises before the request is ever sent)
verdicts.reason:
Overturn. Checked existing-201.txt: this exact candidate isn't in the register (closest neighbors are #41/116 FAIL "SDK-generated idempotency key ... never actually transmitted, dead code" and #62/150 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE "SDK auto-retry-on-timeout double billing" — related but distinct, so not a duplicate submission).

I refetched the pinned commit directly (raw.githubusercontent.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/ad53cac8eeeb1608c162081f883755427ac3a26f/src/anthropic/_base_client.py) and it reproduces the candidate's quote exactly:
`expected_time = maximum_time * max_tokens / 128_000`
`if expected_time > default_time or (max_nonstreaming_tokens and max_tokens > max_nonstreaming_tokens): raise ValueError(...)`
and confirmed the guard sits before `self._post()` in `messages.py`, ahead of the deprecated-model warning. So the source citations are accurate — that isn't where this breaks.

It breaks on mechanism, using exactly the lens I was given: "is there a path where it suppresses ... a call that would NOT have [triggered the thing it's guarding against]?" Yes, and it's built into the formula, not an edge case. Both disjuncts of the guard key off `max_tokens` — the caller's *declared ceiling* — not actual output length, actual latency, or anything the server does:

- The token-cap branch, `max_tokens > max_nonstreaming_tokens` (8192 for Opus-family models per the candidate's own citation of `MODEL_NONSTREAMING_TOKENS`), fires *unconditionally*, with zero reference to `expected_time`. A call with `max_tokens=8200` to Opus that in practice returns 200 tokens and finishes in two seconds is blocked exactly as hard as one that would genuinely run 40 minutes.
- The duration branch computes `expected_time` from the same declared ceiling, not from realized behavior, so it inherits the identical failure mode for any caller who sets `max_tokens` conservatively high (a common defensive habit) while typical completions are short.

For that class of call, the two worlds are not "byte-identical request" vs "byte-identical request" — they are "model reads the prompt, thinks, answers" (no guard) vs "zero bytes ever leave the client, model reads nothing" (with guard). That is precisely THE BAR's FAIL condition — "a different amount of thinking happens" — for every request the heuristic misjudges, and the misjudgment is structural (declared cap ≠ realized behavior), not incidental. PASS_ABSOLUTE requires that adopting the mechanism leave the product unchanged in every case; here the mechanism deterministically converts a working call into a client-side exception whenever the caller's `max_tokens` ceiling is generous relative to actual output, independent of whether the call was ever actually going to be slow. The verdict's own framing — "either it raises (nothing sent) or it doesn't (byte-identical)" — is a false dichotomy: it only compares each branch to itself, never to the counterfactual of what that same call would have done without the guard, which is the comparison THE BAR actually asks for.

Secondary crack: the verdict's "up to 3x savings" corroboration chain (fresh idempotency key per retry ⇒ provider can't dedupe) is not independently cited to verbatim lines the way the guard itself is, and it sits in tension with the register's own existing #41/116 FAIL finding that the SDK's generated idempotency key is dead code and never transmitted at all — if true, "freshness" of a never-sent key is not the operative fact, undermining that leg of the reasoning even though it isn't what the core PASS_ABSOLUTE verdict is supposed to rest on.

Proposed verdict: FAIL, not PASS_ABSOLUTE — the guard is a content-blind proxy (declared max_tokens ceiling) that provably suppresses calls that were never actually going to breach the timeout it's guarding against, and for that subset the amount of model computation goes from "whatever the answer required" to zero.

- Retry/idempotency corroboration verified independently: `APITimeoutError(APIConnectionError)` (exceptions.py) is a real subclass, so `_should_retry_exception`'s `isinstance(current, APIConnectionError)` branch does catch it (line 897), and `_idempotency_key()` is exactly `f"stainless-python-retry-{uuid.uuid4()}"` (line 903), freshly minted per retry at both call sites (1127, 1871). - Went further than the write-up: when the guard does NOT raise, it returns `Timeout(default_time, connect=5.0)` where `default_time` is hardcoded to 600s regardless of max_tokens — i.e. bit-for-bit identical to the pre-existing `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` the guard only fires under. So the non-raising branch isn't just "a byte-identical request," it's a literal no-op. Same holds for TS (`calculateNonstreamingTimeout` always returns `defaultTime`=600000ms when it doesn't throw, which is what the `timeout ?? 600000` fallback would have produced anyway).

TypeScript SDK (fetched current main, both files): the guard IS live — `messages.ts:92` calls `this._client.calculateNonstreamingTimeout(body.max_tokens, maxNonstreamingTokens)` before `this._client.post(...)`, and the cited `client.ts:1426-1438` function matches the quoted formula exactly. Citing it as independent corroboration is sloppy sourcing. It doesn't change the outcome, though, since the line range actually quoted in the reasoning (1426-1438) is the real, wired-in function and matches verbatim. The write-up's dangling "up to 3x savings estimate" is also unsubstantiated in the text given — no derivation shown — but it's a side remark, not load-bearing for the PASS_ABSOLUTE classification itself.

Net: this is a structural, code-verified claim (not "the provider's word") — I read the actual client source myself at a pinned commit and on current main, and in every case where the guard fires it either raises before any request object is built, or computes a timeout value that's provably identical to the default already in effect. verdicts.name: Sidekiq Enterprise Unique Jobs -- default lock key (class, args, queue), computed from the job's own content
verdicts.reason:
Quotes check out verbatim (confirmed against raw HTML at github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Ent-Unique-Jobs, including the "10 minutes... best effort" sentence the WebFetch summarizer had dropped), and the repo is real (13,551 stars, pushed within days). The sourcing isn't the problem — the mechanism analysis is.

1. The claim's load-bearing premise — "for a job whose args ARE the model request payload" — is a self-selected, atypical configuration. Sidekiq's own guidance (and general Sidekiq practice) is to keep job args small (IDs/references), not the full prompt payload, precisely because args are serialized into Redis. In the actually-common pattern, args are a conversation_id/doc_id that gets resolved to the real LLM request AT EXECUTION TIME. Two enqueues with byte-identical (class, args, queue) can then resolve to two different model requests if anything the job reads (conversation history, a document, a retrieved context) changed between pushes — the key is computed from the job's *enqueue-time label*, not from the request that ultimately goes to the model. That is exactly the lens question "is there a path where it suppresses a call that would NOT have been a true duplicate" answered yes, by the vendor's own documented lock semantics, not by speculation.

2. Even granting the claim's own narrow scenario (args = full payload): two different callers who happen to submit a byte-identical prompt to the same class/queue collide on the same lock key. The verified doc text gives push() no response-wiring back to a caller — a rejected duplicate is simply not enqueued. So caller B's independent generation (which at temperature > 0 would ordinarily differ from caller A's) never happens and nothing is returned to B. This is the register's own named failure mode verbatim: "does it collapse independent samples into one frozen sample" — yes, into zero samples for the second caller.

3. Verified default `unique_until: success` holds the lock for the entire retry window ("it will remain locked even if it raises an error and goes into the retry queue"), so the suppression window is not "simultaneous byte-identical pushes" but potentially minutes of in-flight retries — widening, not narrowing, the collision surface described in points 1–2.

4. Register precedent already exists for this exact mechanism class: id 189 in the register is "BullMQ job deduplication (Simple Mode)" — a structurally identical self-hosted, content-keyed, push-time job-queue dedup — and it is recorded FAIL, not PASS_ABSOLUTE. Id 187 (K8s CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Forbid) is the register's only passing analog, and it is explicitly gated as "valid only where the job is provably idempotent" — a bar this claim asserts by stipulation rather than proves, and which the vendor's own "best effort, not a 100% guarantee" language (verified verbatim) affirmatively disclaims.

Net: the claim treats vendor-disclosed unreliability ("best effort, not a 100% guarantee," locks expiring mid-retry, lock scope keyed on enqueue-time args) as merely bounding an already-safe mechanism, when those same disclosures are the register's own evidence that suppressed pushes are not reliably true duplicates of the request that would have reached the model. That is a changed product (fewer, and non-guaranteed-identical, model calls) sold as a saving — FAIL, consistent with the register's BullMQ sibling entry, not PASS_ABSOLUTE.

Reproducing exact substring then swapping the source's comma for a full stop and silently dropping the rest, with no ellipsis, is a verbatim-quoting defect under this register's own rule 2 — minor on its own, but a warning sign to read the whole page rather than grep for pre-selected strings.

That warning is borne out: reading the full stripped page (not just the two grepped quotes) turns up a section the claim never engages, "Lock Context": *"Unique locks are based on (class, queue, args) but as of Sidekiq Enterprise 7.0.3, you can override this context."* The page gives a worked example of a customer-supplied `sidekiq_unique_context` method that deliberately drops an argument from the lock computation — and warns *"if you add a `d` argument, you'd better remember to update the code above or you'll have some strange behavior!"* This directly contradicts the reasoning's central, unqualified claim that "the exact caller-chosen-label failure mode [is] absent here": Sidekiq Enterprise ships a supported mechanism for the lock key to diverge from full job content, which is precisely the caller-controlled-key risk the reasoning says can't happen. The claim's title scopes to "default lock key," but the reasoning body drops that qualifier and asserts the failure mode is structurally impossible — it isn't, on the same page cited as the source.

Separately, the whole chain rests on an unsourced assumption the reasoning states as fact: "for a job whose args ARE the model request payload." Nothing on this Sidekiq wiki page (or anywhere in Sidekiq's docs) mentions LLMs, prompts, or model payloads — this is a generic Redis job-dedup feature, and passing raw prompt text as job args (rather than a reference ID, the more common pattern for keeping Redis payloads small) is an analyst-introduced hypothetical, not a documented or measured behavior. Per this project's own rules, a claim resting on an unverified usage assumption with no measurement to back it should say so rather than be rounded up to PASS_ABSOLUTE.

Given the found override mechanism that undercuts the "never caller-chosen" premise, the unsourced args=payload assumption, and the register's stated bias toward demoting rather than publishing a false pass, I'd downgrade this from PASS_ABSOLUTE to INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE — the structural "no request was ever sent" argument doesn't hold unconditionally the way the reasoning claims, and nothing here rises to a measurement.

verdicts.name: Claude's text watermark (SynthID-style keyed token selection)
verdicts.reason:
Not in existing-201.txt — no watermark entry present, confirmed by full read of the 201-line register before proceeding.

The FAIL reasoning invents a fourth trigger the bar doesn't contain. THE BAR is an explicit three-part disjunction — "does the model read a different sequence of tokens, does a different model answer, or does a different amount of thinking happen?" A keyed-RNG swap at the final sampling step trips none of the three: same input tokens, same model weights/forward pass, same thinking-token budget. The original verdict's operative clause — "which is precisely the register's FAIL condition (a different mechanism decides what gets produced)" — is a self-authored paraphrase substituted for the bar's actual text, not a quote of it, and it's a broader test than the register actually states. That's the same failure mode rule 2 warns about (a restated claim passed off as the standard), just applied to the rubric instead of a source.

Re-fetched the raw HTML directly (not WebFetch's markdown conversion) and grepped every load-bearing sentence verbatim:

- "Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick. That is, the words that Claude picks are still random..." — confirms only the entropy *source* changes, not the vocabulary or distribution the model computes.
- "It belongs to a family of approaches that go back to a proposal by Scott Aaronson in 2022, all of which share the same design principle that we described above—the watermark only changes the source of the randomness used to pick among words." — this is the load-bearing mechanism claim, and it's narrower than the original FAIL treated it: swapping a hardware RNG for a keyed PRF is a standard, decades-old cryptographic substitution (a PRF is computationally indistinguishable from random to anyone without the key) — not obviously the kind of "changed product" the bar's three triggers were written to catch.
- "Claude's text watermark is a version of the SynthID-Text approach published by Google DeepMind in a Nature paper in 2024." + "They found no statistically significant differences from the unwatermarked model. And in a controlled study, human raters comparing watermarked and unwatermarked answers side-by-side saw no difference in quality." — this elevates the equivalence claim above a bare marketing sentence: it's traceable to a peer-reviewed, externally-published measurement (Dathathri et al., Nature 2024) with a live production A/B test and a controlled human-rater study on the underlying algorithm family — closer in kind to the register's own precedent for id 56, "Batch-invariant kernels (Thinking Machines Lab, 'Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference')" — PASS_ABSOLUTE, which also rests on a third party's published technical work rather than the register's own measurement.
- I also checked the "limitations" section for any disclosed quality cost and found none — the only caveats are about detection *confidence* on short passages, not output degradation: "There are limitations to the effectiveness of watermarking... Detecting a watermark also doesn't work well on small samples." Nothing in the source contradicts the equivalence claim.

Where I land short of full PASS: the register gates PASS_ABSOLUTE tightly — "Only a measurement, or a structural argument that no request was ever sent, supports PASS_ABSOLUTE" — and this sweep ran no live traffic, so there's no measurement in hand, and a generation request plainly *was* sent (unlike the "no request sent" client-side cases). The quality-preservation evidence, while real and peer-reviewed, is Google's measurement of Gemini traffic, not this register's own verification of Anthropic's deployment, and it's a statistical "no significant difference" finding on ratings, not a hard bit-identical guarantee (contrast the batch-invariant-kernel case, which is independently checkable via exact byte-equality). That gap is exactly what CONTRACTUAL_ONLY is defined for: "the provider asserts identity and we cannot verify it." Anthropic's "does not impact the quality of Claude's output. To a reader, a watermarked response is indistinguishable from an unwatermarked one" and "produces no extra tokens, the model is the same price to serve and use" are precisely such identity assertions — well-supported by cited third-party research, but still assertions this register did not itself verify.

Net: FAIL was too harsh — it applied a broadened, self-authored version of the bar to a mechanism change (RNG source, not model/input/thinking) that the actual three-part bar doesn't cover, and it treated a peer-reviewed equivalence claim as if it were an unsupported promise. The correct resting place given this project's no-measurement constraint is CONTRACTUAL_ONLY, not FAIL and not PASS_ABSOLUTE.

Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-text-watermark, fetched as raw HTML via curl (not WebFetch's markdown converter) and grepped for exact quote strings on 2026-08-17; local copy at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-angus/39e318fe-66fb-410c-a83c-e148db77ba8b/scratchpad/watermark.html for re-verification.
