verdicts.name: Google Cloud Tasks task-ID deduplication
verdicts.proposedVerdict: PASS_ABSOLUTE — narrowly scoped, on the same pattern as the register's own line 187 (K8s CronJob Forbid: "valid only where the job is provably idempotent"). Scoping clause: valid only where the customer binds the task ID 1:1 to identical request content (e.g., a hash of the request body used as the task ID) so the ID functions as a true idempotency key, not an unrelated business ID.
verdicts.reason:
The original FAIL reasoning quotes the right sentence but draws the wrong conclusion from it. Re-quoting the same source (https://docs.cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/reference/rest/v2/projects.locations.queues.tasks/create, confirmed verbatim via fresh fetch today): "Explicitly specifying a task ID enables task de-duplication. If a task's ID is identical to that of an existing task or a task that was deleted or executed recently then the call will fail with google.rpc.Code.ALREADY_EXISTS."

The FAIL verdict's entire case rests on one scenario: a caller reuses an ID for content that genuinely changed, gets ALREADY_EXISTS, and "either loses the new content or must mint a new ID, defeating the dedup." But look at what actually happens in that scenario: the call FAILS with a hard, synchronous error. It does not silently serve the old content, silently merge, or silently proceed with the stale task. THE BAR's own test is about silent substitution — "a changed product sold as a saving" — the customer being told they got X and getting Y without knowing it. A loud, typed error that forces the caller to notice and re-mint an ID is the opposite of that; it is the mechanism refusing to let semantic drift happen unnoticed. That's a bad-configuration footgun (don't reuse IDs across non-identical content), not a property of the dedup mechanism misbehaving — exactly the kind of misclassification the advocate brief asks me to check for.

Look instead at the mechanism's behavior in its intended use (ID bound to content, i.e. a real idempotency key, which is what "hashed strings for the task id" nudges toward): a second create() with the same ID for the same logical request fails outright, meaning no new task object is ever created. Cloud Tasks only dispatches tasks that exist in the queue; a create that returns ALREADY_EXISTS means nothing was added to dispatch. That is the structural "no request was ever sent" argument the rules explicitly carve out as sufficient for PASS_ABSOLUTE without a measurement — the duplicate never reaches the point (worker dispatch) that would invoke the LLM at all. Cloud Tasks is also squarely in scope under "unless the customer runs the gateway themselves": the queue and the worker that calls the model are both the customer's own infrastructure.

This lines up with the register's existing entries rather than contradicting them: AWS Bedrock CreateModelInvocationJob's clientRequestToken (line 36) already passed as PASS_ABSOLUTE for the identical create-call-with-ID-token shape. AWS SQS FIFO MessageDeduplicationId (line 190) only got CONTRACTUAL_ONLY — but that's because SQS's own docs hedge that "in rare cases" a message can still be delivered more than once, and a duplicate send returns a soft 200 rather than a typed rejection, so the caller has no independently verifiable signal. Cloud Tasks does the opposite: a hard ALREADY_EXISTS with no such hedge anywhere in its docs (confirmed on the fresh fetch — the only caveats are latency and a 24h/9d ID-reuse window, not "may occasionally double-create"). That puts it structurally closer to Bedrock's token and to the register's K8s CronJob Forbid entry (line 187), which the register already accepts as PASS_ABSOLUTE under a "provably idempotent" scoping — the exact same scoping this candidate needs and can carry.

One honest gap: today's fetch could not find documentation language confirming the create-then-dedup check is atomic/race-free — worth flagging rather than rounding up, and it is the reason I'm proposing the same narrow, precedent-matched scoping the CronJob entry uses rather than an unscoped pass. But that gap is a documentation silence, not a stated weaker guarantee (unlike SQS's explicit hedge), so it doesn't drag this to CONTRACTUAL_ONLY on its own.

Checked against existing-201.txt (grep for "cloud task"/"dedup"/"idempoten"/"cronjob"/"forbid"): no existing entry covers Google Cloud Tasks task-ID dedup specifically, so this is not a restatement of lines 36, 38, 187, 189, or 190 — those are the comparison set, not duplicates.

The flagship quote is exact, character for character: "LiteLLM calls Headroom in-process during the pre_call step to rewrite the messages, then forwards the compressed payload to the upstream LLM. The client and the upstream LLM provider do not talk to Headroom directly." That is a vendor description of a live, synchronous rewrite in the request path for every request the guardrail is attached to — not a stored replay, not an identity claim we have to trust: the vendor is affirmatively describing non-identity (that is the entire value proposition of a "compression" product; its own meta description says "so you get the same answers at a fraction of the tokens," i.e., fewer tokens, not the same tokens). A difference-claim backed by the mechanism's own documented design doesn't need a live measurement to support FAIL the way an identity-claim would need one to support PASS_ABSOLUTE — the asymmetry in the rules works in FAIL's favor here, not against it.

I looked for a CronJob-Forbid-style narrower scoping (a structural, provable case where this specific technique is a no-op) and did not find one that survives. The strongest candidate is the "Why requests_compressed can be 0" section, which I confirmed verbatim: "Headroom protects two message types by default... user / system messages, unless ENV HEADROOM_COMPRESS_USER_MESSAGES=1 is set. Most Claude Code traffic is user role, so a default deployment compresses none of it. Messages with an Anthropic cache_control marker, always. Compressing them would break prompt-cache byte matching. No override exists." This is real and the candidate's flagship reliance on it is fine, but it doesn't earn a scoped PASS the way CronJob-Forbid's idempotency does: idempotency is a provable structural property of the job itself; "compresses none of it" here is a contingent fact about traffic shape (Anthropic tool_result blocks happen to live inside user-role messages) that only holds in a default configuration where the product provides zero benefit. Nobody deploys Headroom for its advertised purpose and leaves it in the state where it touches nothing — the moment it's configured to do what it's sold to do (compress tool outputs / RAG / file-reads / DB-results, none of which are in either protected category), the model reads different tokens. A no-op default is not a meaningful pass scope for a compression product any more than "don't enable the feature" would be for any other technique in this register.

One correction to the candidate's own writeup, found independently, that it did not self-flag: the reasoning states "system/tool-role messages are compressed by default but user-role messages are not unless HEADROOM_COMPRESS_USER_MESSAGES=1 is set" — but the verbatim text groups them together, "user / system messages, unless ENV HEADROOM_COMPRESS_USER_MESSAGES=1 is set," meaning system-role is protected by default alongside user-role, not compressed by default as the candidate claimed. This doesn't change the verdict (tool-role/RAG/file-read/DB-result content — the actual compression target — is protected in neither category, by either name), but it's a second citation-fidelity slip beyond the fabricated splice the candidate already caught itself on, worth fixing before entry.

verdicts.reason:
Checked for duplication first: scanned all 201 rows in existing-201.txt for "context editing," "clear_tool_uses," "84%," or any tool-result-stripping mechanism. Nearest neighbors are id 73 "Mid-conversation tool changes (tool_addition/removal/defer_loading)" (FAIL) and id 157 "Zombie context in scheduled/cron agents" (FAIL) — both distinct mechanisms (schema mutation and stale-context accumulation, not server-side deletion-and-placeholder-substitution of tool results). Not a restatement of anything in the register.

Re-fetched both cited URLs directly (not relying on the prior pass's quotes) and confirmed both load-bearing quotes verbatim, from raw content, not paraphrase:
- Mechanism, from platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing: "When activated, the API automatically clears the oldest tool results in chronological order. The API replaces each cleared result with placeholder text indicating to Claude that it was removed. By default, only tool results are cleared." — exact match.
- The "84%" figure, from claude.com/blog/context-management: "In a 100-turn web search evaluation, context editing enabled agents to complete workflows that would otherwise fail due to context exhaustion—while reducing token consumption by 84%." — exact match, and it's a token-consumption figure Anthropic itself frames as the payoff, so "sold as a saving" in the entry title is not the register's own spin — it echoes the source's own framing.

Then tried hard to find a narrower scoping that flips this, using the CronJob Forbid precedent (id 187, PASS_ABSOLUTE, "valid only where the job is provably idempotent") as the template: is there a configuration of clear_tool_uses_20250919 where the substitution is effectively identity? No — placeholder text can never be byte-identical to the tool result it replaces; that's the entire mechanism. This differs structurally from CronJob Forbid, where skipping a scheduled invocation *can* be a no-op if the job is idempotent. There is no idempotent mode of "delete the real content and write a marker in its place." The one genuine edge case — the trigger threshold never being crossed in a given conversation, so no edit ever fires — is already correctly identified in the reasoning and correctly treated as a per-conversation dormancy fact rather than a property of the feature, exactly parallel to how the register would (correctly) still mark a feature FAIL even though it's inert below its own threshold. No other rows in the register get a pass for "hasn't fired yet."

Checked whether this was mis-scored as a performance/measurement claim needing live traffic (which this project explicitly cannot supply — no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, no measured rows). It isn't: the FAIL bar question ("does the model read a different sequence of tokens") is answered by the documented mechanism itself — the *existence* of chronological deletion-and-substitution — not by the 84% or 29%/39% figures, which are performance/efficiency claims layered on top. The mechanism fact is a structural argument sourced straight from the docs, exactly the kind of evidence the bar treats as sufficient for a definitive verdict without a measurement (compare: "a structural argument that no request was ever sent" is explicitly allowed to support PASS_ABSOLUTE without measurement; a structural argument that content plainly was altered is the mirror case for FAIL).

Checked for a CONTRACTUAL_ONLY reading (documentation asserting identity, capped since unverifiable) — doesn't fit, because the documentation is asserting non-identity (an active content-editing operation), not claiming the request was left untouched. There's no identity claim here to be skeptical of; the provider is describing the exact opposite.

No thread pulls this below FAIL. The entry's quote is genuinely verbatim, the URLs check out, the reasoning's own carve-out is correctly scoped and doesn't broaden the verdict, and there's no idempotent/degenerate general case the way CronJob Forbid has. Upheld as FAIL.
